text: Kashmir Martyrs' Day (Urdu: یومِ شہداءِ کشمیر, Kashmiri: کٲشِرؠ شَہیٖدَن ہُینٛد دۄہ) or Kashmir Day was an official state holiday observed in Kashmir to commemorate 21 Muslims killed on 13 July 1931 by Dogra forces of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir in British India. On that day, Kashmiri Muslims were offering prayers outside the Srinagar Central Jail, where Abdul Qadeer, who had urged Kashmiris to resist the rule of Hari Singh, was present. As the crowd grew restless and the Islamic call to prayer began, the Dogra army opened fire, killing the first muezzin who was giving the Azan. Another muezzin attempted to continue the prayer and was also shot dead, and in total 23 people were killed in attempts to complete the Azan. The bodies were buried in the graveyard attached to the Shrine of Khwaja Bahawuddin Naqshbandi (Ziyarat Naqshband Sahab) in Srinagar, which is now known as Mazar-e-Shuhada or the Martyrs' Graveyard. The day was removed as an official holiday of Jammu and Kashmir by the Government of India in December 2019, although the Government of Pakistan continues to mark it. GM Lone, in Kashmir Life, identifies four incidents that led to the tragedy: a Hindu businessman in Udhampur converted to Islam, had his property taken and was denied inheritance under a 1882 Dogra decree; on 29 April 1931, Muslims were stopped from delivering Khutbah after police intervention, leading to a protest at the main masjid and increased unrest; on 4 June 1931, police constable Fazal Dad Khan’s copy of Panjsurah was thrown away by a sub-inspector, prompting him to go to the mosque; and on 20 June 1931, Quran leaves were found in a public lavatory. Prem Nath Bazaz, in "Inside Kashmir" (1941), stated that the mass agitation leading to 13 July was driven by Muslim discontent and that those who died at the jail gate fought against an unsympathetic government. Abdul Qadeer Khan, an employee of Major Butt of the Yorkshire Regiment, had been attending protest meetings and at Khanqah-i-Maula on 21 June 1931 delivered an impromptu speech, which was recorded by authorities and led to his arrest on 25 June for sedition and inciting riot under the Ranbir Penal Code. His trial began on 4 July in Srinagar, with large Muslim crowds gathering to witness it. On 13 July, the trial continued at Srinagar Jail, where about 160 police officers, including at least 31 armed with guns, were present. Around 4,000 to 5,000 people gathered, were denied entry, but about 200 entered peacefully. Khan’s lawyers addressed the crowd, who agreed to leave after the noon prayer. At noon, Muslims lined up for prayers; when officials including the District Magistrate and Superintendent of Police arrived, slogans such as "Allah-o-Akbar," "Islam Zindabad," and "Abdul Qadeer Zindabad" were shouted. As the call to prayer began, Governor Raizada Trilok Chand ordered police to open fire, killing the first muezzin instantly and shooting dead the second muezzin attempting to finish the Azan, after which police fired indiscriminately. A gun was snatched by a crowd member and he was shot dead by a policeman. According to the Dalal Inquiry Commission, 180 rounds were fired, resulting in 17 Muslims killed on the spot and 40 seriously injured, five of whom died later; The Hindu, Daily Tribune (28 July 1931), reported 21 Muslim deaths. GS Raghavan, in The Warning From Kashmir, described the event as a mob storming the jail, forcing open gates, and stoning officials and police, with the District Magistrate ordering fire, which led to further unrest and looting. The crowd later resumed stoning and was dispersed with a lathi charge and cavalry pursuit. The bodies were buried at the Shrine of Khwaja Bahawuddin Naqshbandi, now known as Mazar-e-Shuhada. Jyoti Bhusan Das Gupta wrote that modern Kashmir's 'freedom movement' began on 13 July 1931, while Prem Nath Bazaz called 13 July 1931 the most important day in contemporary Kashmir's history, marking the start of an open struggle for independence and freedom. Sheikh Abdullah compared the day to the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre, and Chitralekha Zutshi emphasized the incident's multi-casualty nature and its roots in socio-economic and socio-political crises. In protest, the Reading Room Party announced a statewide shutdown, and at a public meeting at the Martyrs' Graveyard, Sheikh Abdullah declared 13 July as Martyr's Day. This unrest led to arrests of Sheikh Abdullah and Chaudhry Ghulam Abbas. The aftermath prompted Maharaja Hari Singh to appoint a commission chaired by B J Glancy to examine Muslim grievances and to democratize the monarchy, resulting in the proposal of a legislative assembly, which was established in 1934.
